questions.answer: A physical quantity consists of a numerical magnitude and a unit.
questions.unit_policy: No unit is required because the response names the two parts rather than reporting a measured value.

marking_points.text: States numerical magnitude or numerical value
States unit

questions.unit_policy: No written unit is required because the learner selects one complete option.

marking_points.text: Selects 5 kg as a reasonable mass estimate for a loaded school bag

option_feedback.A: 0.005 kg is far lighter than the books and equipment in a loaded bag.
option_feedback.B: 0.5 kg may fit a nearly empty light bag, but is too small for the stated loaded bag.
option_feedback.C: Correct. Several kilograms is a believable scale for a bag containing books and equipment.
option_feedback.D: 500 kg is far beyond a mass that one student could carry.

questions.unit_policy: No written unit is required because the learner selects one complete option.

marking_points.text: Selects 0.2 s as a reasonable time estimate for one blink

option_feedback.A: 0.002 s is too brief for the visible closing and opening movement of an eyelid.
option_feedback.B: Correct. A fraction of one second is the believable scale for one blink.
option_feedback.C: 20 s would make a single blink last long enough to notice as an extended eye closure.
option_feedback.D: 2000 s is many minutes and is not the scale of one blink.

questions.unit_policy: No written unit is required because the learner selects one complete option.

marking_points.text: Selects 150 cm³ as a reasonable volume estimate for a large apple

option_feedback.A: 1.5 cm³ is smaller than a small fingertip-sized object and is far too small for an apple.
option_feedback.B: 15 cm³ is still much smaller than the 125 cm³ benchmark cube.
option_feedback.C: Correct. A value near the 125 cm³ cube, with some allowance for the apple's size and shape, is reasonable.
option_feedback.D: 15 000 cm³ is one hundred times 150 cm³ and would hold many apples.

questions.answer: A student height is a suitable benchmark. A classroom door is a little taller than most students, so an estimate near 2 m is reasonable. Accept a justified estimate from 1.8 m to 2.5 m.
accepted_alternatives: A familiar room-height or metre-length benchmark may replace student height if the comparison supports a value from 1.8 m to 2.5 m.
questions.unit_policy: The estimate must be reported in m as requested.
questions.tolerance: Accept 1.8 m to 2.5 m inclusive when supported by a physically sensible comparison.

marking_points.text: Names a physically relevant height or length benchmark
Compares the classroom door sensibly with the chosen benchmark
States a justified door-height estimate from 1.8 m to 2.5 m
Includes m as the unit of the estimated height

questions.answer: Estimated bundle mass = 12 x 0.25 kg = 3.0 kg, reported suitably as about 3 kg. The answer is approximate because 0.25 kg is an estimated single-book mass. A bundle of 12 books can be lifted by one person but feels much heavier than one book, which is consistent with a mass of a few kilograms.
accepted_alternatives: An equivalent physical check comparing the bundle with three 1 kg objects is acceptable.
questions.unit_policy: kg is required with the bundle mass. Equivalent correctly converted units are accepted only if both value and reasoning are consistent.
questions.tolerance: Exact calculation from the supplied benchmark: 3.0 kg; about 3 kg is the preferred estimate report.

marking_points.text: Multiplies the estimated single-book mass by 12
Obtains and reports the bundle mass as about 3 kg
Explains that the result remains approximate because 0.25 kg is an estimated benchmark
Gives a relevant physical comparison for a bundle of 12 books
Uses the physical comparison to support a mass on the scale of a few kilograms

questions.answer: Estimated volume = 40 cm x 30 cm x 25 cm = 30 000 cm³. The numerical magnitude is 30 000 and the unit is cm³. The bare number is incomplete because it does not state the measurement unit. A 10 cm cube has volume 1000 cm³, so the box volume is equivalent to 30 such cube-volumes, giving 30 x 1000 cm³ = 30 000 cm³ as an independent scale check.
accepted_alternatives: 3.0 x 10^4 cm³ with the same magnitude-unit identification and cube check
questions.unit_policy: cm³ is required with the volume because all supplied approximate dimensions are in cm.
questions.tolerance: Exact product of the supplied approximate dimensions: 30 000 cm³. Equivalent scientific notation is accepted.

marking_points.text: Multiplies the three approximate dimensions 40 cm, 30 cm and 25 cm
Obtains the estimated box volume as 30 000 cm³
Identifies 30 000 as the numerical magnitude and cm³ as the unit
Explains that the bare number is incomplete because it does not state the measurement unit
Uses a 10 cm cube as 1000 cm³ and shows that the box volume is equivalent to 30 such cube-volumes
Shows that the cube check gives the same scale of 30 000 cm³
